why: With the wars, laws and ways of living of tranche B added to the machines of tranche A, Wells moves ahead of E. E. Smith: 192 of his ideas from 27 books came true, for 549.5 points to Smith's 467.5. The scientific romances still score, with weightless travelers and a sealed cabin of breathable air in The First Men in the Moon (1900), as on Vostok 1 and Voskhod 1. The lead comes from the forecaster. When the Sleeper Wakes (1899) runs the trade of the whole world on one currency of council cheques (the euro, 1999; Sweden's nearly cashless shops, 2015), Anticipations (1901) foresees a federal Europe (the Maastricht Treaty, 1993) and the passing of Britain's mercantile and naval lead to the United States (1945), and A Modern Utopia (1905) has the state limit births (Singapore, 1972).

Godfrey Sweven was the pen name of John Macmillan Brown, a Scottish-born professor in New Zealand. Limanora, the Island of Progress (1903) tours a utopia run on applied science, and it scores on 88 ideas, the most of any single work: a tidal power station (the Rance, 1966), liquid air stored as grid energy (a plant near Manchester, 2018), a gas that puts crowds to sleep, implants that sharpen the senses, and screening of the whole population for disease.

Utopia (1516) describes an imagined island, and among its customs is a painless death for the incurably ill who choose it, urged on them by the priests and magistrates: those persuaded "take opium, and by that means die without pain." Exit Deutsche Schweiz, a Swiss right-to-die society, helped its first patient to die in 1985, 469 years later. The judges scored the match 0.75, and no prediction in a modern work earns more points. Locke's lunar meteorites, 148 years early and judged closer at 0.875, are second.

The Achievements of Luther Trant (1910) follows a young psychologist who solves crimes with laboratory instruments, and 48% of its 62 predictions came true at a judged 0.5 or closer, the best record of any author with 50 or more. Trant's blood-pressure lie detector was put to use by the Berkeley police in 1921, and the book's word-association tests and other methods of psychological detection followed.

George Griffith, a Victorian journalist and writer of future-war serials, averages 58.0 points over his six books in the corpus. The Angel of the Revolution (1893) powers London from the Thames tides through turbines (the Rance station, 1966) and lifts its airships straight up on fan-wheels (the Harrier, 1969); Olga Romanoff (1894) runs trains at two hundred miles an hour (the TGV, 1981); The World Peril of 1910 (1906) aims a gun at a comet headed for the Earth (NASA's DART, 2022); and A Honeymoon in Space (1901) has a gas that leaves people insensible. His wars and revolutions, scored in tranche B, carry him past Richard M. Elam.

Verne's books before 1900 score 401 points on 125 ideas, the most of any nineteenth-century writer. His moon travelers float weightless in their projectile, as Gagarin did in 1961; they wear spacesuits, pass the point where Earth's and the Moon's gravity cancel, and see a second small moon of the Earth. Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863) imagines hydrogen and oxygen as fuel and a searchlight carried aloft.

Wells's books of 1900 to 1945 score 402.7 points on 150 ideas, just ahead of E. E. Smith's 385.0 once the social predictions count. The First Men in the Moon (1900) has weightlessness and a sealed cabin of breathable air; Anticipations (1901) has a federal Europe and cities grown into one continuous urban region; A Modern Utopia (1905) has a state that limits births and households that eat together in public halls; and The World Set Free leaves its battlefields "sprinkled with radiant matter", as Castle Bravo's fallout left Rongelap in 1954.

Leinster wrote for six decades; his books from 1946 on score 349 points on 156 ideas, the most of the postwar era. Med Service (1957) has a gas that puts a crowd to sleep, as Russian forces used in Moscow in 2002; If You Was a Moklin (1951) has private spaceships; The Last Space Ship (1949) has weapons that destroy objects in orbit, and Pariah Planet (1961) teaches people in their sleep.

Anticipations (1901) is Wells's book-length forecast of the twentieth century, and with tranche B it outscores T. Baron Russell's A Hundred Years Hence, the tranche-A winner, by 159.9 points to 131.4: the nations of Europe drawing into a union (Maastricht, 1993), cities spreading into a continuous region from Lille to Kiel (the Boston-to-Washington belt by 1950), the transfer of Britain's mercantile and naval lead to the United States (1945), and, darker, a state that kills those it judges unfit (Nazi Germany, 1939).

With tranche B, Utopia edges past Bacon's New Atlantis, the tranche-A winner, by 71.7 points to 70.9, on fewer but older hits: money abolished (the Khmer Rouge, 1975), private property abolished (Soviet Russia, 1918), support as of right for workers too old or ill to labor (Germany's sickness insurance, 1883), meals taken together in public halls instead of at home (China's communes, 1958) and a painless death for those who ask for it (Switzerland, 1985).

Democracy in America (1835 and 1840) wins among the works of politics and philosophy on 12 ideas. Tocqueville saw the Anglo-Americans covering the continent (the 1890 census found no frontier line left), the United States and Russia each "marked out by the will of Heaven to sway the destinies of half the globe" (the Cold War, 1947), and democratic peoples trading the classics for practical and scientific schooling. He also expected false diamonds to be made that could not be told from real ones (General Electric, 1957).

The Mahabharata reached its final form by about 400 CE, so every idea it shares with the modern world counts at the 500-year cap. It wins on breadth, not precision: 30 ideas, all but one judged 0.5 or less. A conch blast that leaves whole armies without strength (a ship drove off pirates with an acoustic device in 2005), a weapon that sends the foe to sleep, a poison neutralized by another poison (Calmette's antivenom, 1895), and yogic control of the breath and body. Lucian's True History, with its flight on borrowed wings and its eyes that can be taken out, is second.

Kipling's two stories of a world run by the Aerial Board of Control, "With the Night Mail" and "As Easy as A.B.C.", imagine the instruments of airline flying in detail: a recorder of the flight, a moving map in the cockpit, and zones where instruments and engines fail. They are collected in Actions and Reactions (1909) and A Diversity of Creatures (1917).

Wallace's stories of the 1950s put robots to work as nannies, waiters and companions, and The Man Who Was Six (1954) imagines immersive virtual reality 36 years before VPL sold the first headsets. Delay in Transit (1952) has a rewritable electronic page, which E Ink first showed in a shop in 1999.

Smith's heroes carry pocket wireless telephones in 1928, 55 years before the first commercial cellular call, choose films to watch on demand, talk mind to mind through a machine, and meet in three-dimensional projection.

Senarens wrote most of the Frank Reade dime novels, whose boy inventor builds a new machine for every adventure. Frank Reade Jr.'s Submarine Boat (1893) goes to the North Pole under the ice (USS Skate surfaced there in 1959), his Air Wonder hangs from rotors (the Flettner Fl 282, 1942), the airship of The Transient Lake (1896) seals its cabin for the thin air above the clouds (the Boeing 307, 1940), and the submarine of The Sunken Isthmus (1896) makes its own oxygen and destroys its bad air, as USS Seawolf did on a 60-day submerged cruise in 1958. He edges Griffith by one point.
Verne imagined hydrogen and oxygen as fuel in Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863), heat stored from one season to the next in Topsy-Turvy (1889), and an electric aircraft in Robur the Conqueror (1886).

Limanora's islanders sharpen and add to their senses with implants, put each other to sleep with a spray or a current, stun without killing, and screen everyone for disease, all ideas that came true from 1936 to 2004.

Smith armed his heroes with microwave weapons (a US Air Force source, 1988), cutting beams that slice metal (the first laser cutting machine, 1970), sleep gas and powered armor, the exoskeleton DARPA's BLEEX showed in 2004.

From the Earth to the Moon and All Around the Moon get the physics of the trip right more often than any other books: weightlessness, spacesuits, the point where Earth's and the Moon's gravity cancel, and a second small moon of the Earth.

Wells takes the environment award from Verne by less than a point, 37.8 to 37.1. In "The Star" (1897) a body from outer space passes the Earth and brings earthquakes, floods and rising heat, a cosmic catastrophe of the kind confirmed when the Chicxulub crater was tied to the end of the dinosaurs (1991). The World Set Free leaves its battlefields radioactive for years (Rongelap, 1954), and in Tono-Bungay (1909) a character proposes letting the Mediterranean into the Dead Sea valley, water engineering on the scale of China's South-North diversion (2013).

When the Sleeper Wakes (1899) wakes its sleeper into a London where the trade of the whole world runs on one currency of council cheques, which counts twice: one money across many states (the euro, 1999) and cash giving way to accounts (Sweden, 2015). Anticipations (1901) moves the world's mercantile lead to the United States (1945), and a story in The Stolen Bacillus (1895) imagines diamonds made so cheaply that they become "as common as coal" (General Electric, 1957). Edward Bellamy is a close second.

With tranche B the society and politics domain counts the social and political predictions themselves, and Wells leads it by almost three to one, 116.6 points to Griffith's 39.8. A Modern Utopia (1905) limits births and sends households to communal tables, When the Sleeper Wakes (1899) makes English the language of the world, and Anticipations (1901) unites Europe. His tranche-A hits are here too: machines that count votes and a central register of every citizen.

The Time Machine (1895) treats time as a fourth dimension of space thirteen years before Minkowski's lecture, and other stories add synthetic diamonds (General Electric, 1957), clothing that changes color, and buildings put up by machine.

This award, for wars, revolutions, laws, institutions and ways of living, exists because of tranche B, and Wells wins it with more than twice the runner-up's score: 186.2 points from 65 ideas to Griffith's 77.8. His social forecasts came true across the century: one currency for many nations (1999), a union of Europe (1993), the state limiting births (Singapore, 1972), households eating in public halls (China's communes, 1958) and English as the common language of the world (about 1950).

From 1516 to 1985 is 469 years, the longest lead of any prediction in a modern work judged 0.75 or closer: Utopia's painless death for those who choose it, which Exit Deutsche Schweiz first gave a patient in Switzerland. The next three are early-modern too: Cyrano de Bergerac's staged rocket (287 years), the hearing "helps" of Bacon's New Atlantis (273) and the state-matched breeding of Campanella's City of the Sun (267).

By date of publication, Verne was the first author in the corpus to predict 71 ideas that later came true, more than anyone else. All Around the Moon (1870) alone has spacesuits, the point between Earth and Moon where their pulls cancel (where ISEE-3 was parked in 1978), and a second, tiny moon of the Earth (2006 RH120). Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863) burns hydrogen and oxygen for power, as the Centaur rocket stage did a century later.

Simon Newcomb, the leading American astronomer of his day, wrote in 1906 that no combination of known substances, machinery and forces could make a practical machine to carry men long distances through the air. Within four years, airplanes were carrying people and mail across cities and countries. A check of all 138 skeptics the pipeline flagged in both tranches confirmed that his was a real "never" that came true, and it was refuted the soonest.

In "The Jameson Satellite" (Amazing Stories, 1931) a professor has his body put into orbit around the Earth after his death to preserve it, and the story dates the launch to 1958. Sputnik 1 went up on 4 October 1957, one year early, 26 years after the story was printed.

Intelligent life on other worlds is the future the corpus expects most and has not received: 540 books imagine it, from Cyrano de Bergerac's moon voyage of 1657, whose narrator already believes "the fixed Stars are also Suns which have Planets about them", to the pulps. Planets of other stars were found in 1995; their inhabitants have not been. Next come crewed ships to the stars (511 books) and telepathy (480 books), the tranche-A edition's winner.
